bodyOriginal.text: Furniture company IKEA has launched the limited-edition Konstrunda collection, an assortment of furniture and homeware objects that reimagine collectible design from the likes of Andu Masebo at an affordable price point.
Konstrunda, or Art Tour, consists of 22 pieces by seven designers, including work from Masebo , Italian designer Emanuele Stamuli and Swedish talents like Lisa Hilland , all for under £200.

IKEA has launched a collection of collectible design and art "By elevating everyday objects into art pieces, we give people the opportunity to live with art, rather than just viewing it from a distance in a museum," Konstrunda creative leader Karin Gustavsson told Dezeen. "We have the ability to offer this at a price that people can afford."
"Konstrunda can be that entry point for a younger person who is just beginning to collect pieces for the home."

London-based designer Andu Masebo created a side table for the collection The objects range from a £19 black-and-white vase designed by architect Emanuele Stamuli to Masebo 's £149 Konstrunda side table, wrapped in a chunky frame reminiscent of the Tubular Chair that first catapulted him to international attention.
The London designer also contributed two geometric stools that can double as side tables or plinths, one made of raw pine and the other covered in bright blue paint.

Swedish artist Lisa Reiser created mouth-blown glass vases The IKEA collaboration marks Masebo's latest foray into low-cost mass production following his show at Unit.d gallery in London, where he created affordable, everyday objects from folded sheet metal .

"Scalability has always been something I've been interested in engaging with," he told Dezeen. "I want to make work that is rich in depth, but I also want it to be felt by people outside of my own bubble."
"To make something that can be considered art, that can also be accessible is a really interesting challenge to consider."

Lisa Hilland contributed a bright orange sculpture and pine wood stool Swedish artist Lisa Reiser created mouthblown glass vases informed by her own daydreams for the collection, including a bright-green "gummy candy" version, while Hilland contributed a pinewood stool and a bent orange sculpture.
Designers Ingrid Leander and Igor Holtermann worked together on boldly patterned cushions and a rug informed by zebra crossings and caution banners they observed in the Stockholm streetscape.

Read: "IKEA has challenged the rest of the design world" In-house designer Akanksha Deo hoped to address the contemporary loneliness epidemic with two expressive vessels, one of which resembles a "character" made of stacked blocks to give people a sense of companionship.
Despite their functionality, Gustavsson refers to all of the pieces in the collection as "art objects", since she says the furniture giant doesn't see "art and design as separate worlds".

Ingrid Leander and Igor Holtermann took cues from Stockholm's streetscape "This brief was about artistic expression, not about beginning with a functional need or everyday challenge that needed to be solved," said Gustavsson.
"We at IKEA feel that collectible design shouldn't have a barrier to entry, that to collect things you love and that speak to you should be available for the many."

IKEA also recently released its 2026 PS collection , which is similarly playful and affordable. Writer Debika Ray recently explored the impact of the collection , while Dezeen discussed if the price point was "too good to be true" on a recent podcast .

articles.titleOriginal: When bike brand Brompton needed a refresh, Studio Blackburn didn't mess around—they headed straight to the factory floor
articles.summaryOriginal: Iconic bicycle manufacturer Brompton needed a global brand platform. But Studio Blackburn didn't just design a system. They went to the source and cut metal letters next to the machines that build...

bodyOriginal.text: Iconic bicycle manufacturer Brompton needed a global brand platform. But Studio Blackburn didn't just design a system. They went to the source and cut metal letters next to the machines that build the bikes.

It's no secret that we're big fans of Brompton at Creative Boom (watch our exclusive video Inside Brompton's London Factory if you don't believe me.) Their funky folding bike has been a design icon since 1975, and attracted the kind of cult following most brands can only dream of.

So when Studio Blackburn was brought in to build a scalable, digital-first brand platform for Brompton's global expansion across Europe, the USA and Asia, the brief wasn't "make Brompton interesting." It was already interesting. The brief was simply to take the place cyclists have in their hearts for Brompton, and amplify it around the world.

The first smart decision Studio Blackburn made was to take the iconic Brompton logo and its triptych symbol and… do absolutely nothing to change them. In a world where companies often rebrand stuff without any obvious reason to (*cough Insta- *cough -gram), there's something admirably confident in that level of creative insight.

The problem wasn't the logotype itself; it was what happened when teams needed to use it in international markets. It had never been extended into a full character set, so internal teams were having to improvise. The result, across retail, online, CRM and advertising, was fragmentation.

Studio Blackburn's solution was Brompton Slab: a bespoke headline typeface developed in partnership with type designer Sam White. The team adjusted the letterforms to ensure long-form legibility across global languages.

Now, here's the bit that shows just how well Studio Blackburn understood the brand. To launch Brompton Slab, the team went to the factory in Greenford, where the bikes are actually built by hand, and cut oversized metal letters.
The resulting images are some of the most striking brand photography you'll see this year. The letters don't look out of place at all; they look like they belong there, which makes perfect sense.
The typeface was developed from the logo; the logo came from the factory; ergo, the typeface belongs on the factory floor. It's circular logic, and Studio Blackburn pulled it off masterfully.
Underpinning the whole system is a single phrase: Life Unfolded. It's clever because it works on multiple levels at once, without trying too hard.
It nods to the product's defining feature as a folding bike. It also captures how Brompton opens up the city to riders, turning a boring commute into an adventure.

The motion principles follow the same logic. Inspired by the distinctive mechanical "final flick" of the rear wheel as the bike unfolds, Studio Blackburn built a motion architecture that shifts between what they describe as smooth "3-speed" UI transitions and dynamic "12-speed" editorial layouts.

Colour-wise, Brompton Blue, a high-visibility, industrial hue directly inspired by the factory visit, serves as a visual anchor across every touchpoint, with the flexibility to shift into custom palettes for collaborations.

The more you look into this work, the more impressed you get with what Studio Blackburn has achieved here. Namely, taking a brand that already had enormous equity, acknowledging what shouldn't be changed, and building the infrastructure around that, allowing the company to grow properly across the globe.

There's a version of this project that could have gone very differently. A global redesign of a beloved British icon, in the wrong hands, could have stripped out all the personality and left you with nothing but polished but empty blandness. Studio Blackburn's refresh of Brompton does the exact opposite. Brompton has been making things properly in London since 1975. Turns out their agency of choice does the same.

bodyOriginal.text: International studio Open Architecture drew on Lina Bo Bardi 's own designs when creating The Poetics of Survival, the first major exhibition of the architect's work in China .
The studio centred the exhibition, which is on show at the Power Station of Art (PSA) gallery in Shanghai, around "a single continuous curve".

bodyOriginal.alt: Lina Bo Bardi exhibition in Shanghai

bodyOriginal.text: The Poetics of Survival is the first major exhibition in China of Lina Bo Bardi's work This shape was created by using hanging linen curtains in the rectangular art gallery, where they surround rectilinear display cases custom-made by Open Architecture .
In PSA's lobby, the studio created a replica of the indoor pond designed by Bardi for the SESC Pompéia community centre in 1977, though they didn't make it as permanent as the original.

bodyOriginal.alt: Pond at Lina Bo Bardi exhibition

bodyOriginal.text: It features an indoor pond that replicates a Bardi design "In Lina's version, the pond embodies the São Francisco River, which runs across Brazil," the studio said.

"It was 'transported' to Shanghai at its original scale. However, in the PSA gallery, it is not embedded into the ground as it does at SESC Pompéia, but instead, appears to levitate slightly above the ground surface."

Read: "Experience of Brasília" evoked at interior installation in Niemeyer's São Paulo pavilion To add interest, Open Architecture filled the pond with pebbles in a variety of sizes and added a water feature that sees water drip from the ceiling.
In the main exhibition spaces, the studio created freestanding "islands" for the architectural models and other key exhibition pieces.

Open Architecture created custom-made displays and furniture The exhibition was divided into nine spaces, which highlight Bardi's work through a mix of media – including sketches, photographs and videos.
The Poetics of Survival features large-scale projections that move across the linen curtains, creating a dynamic feel, and the exhibition texts are also silkscreen-printed directly onto the linen.

As well as the display cabinets, Open Architecture custom-made some furniture pieces for the space, including a bench made from wooden beams and a glass, latticed wood and concrete divider in the lobby.
The studio designed a beam-like bench for the exhibition The studio hoped that the design for The Poetics of Survival will give visitors a feel for what inspired Bardi.

"Presenting Lina's work within a setting that is informed by her own design ethos and sensibility allows audiences to encounter not only her work, but also get a sense of the world that inspired it," Open Architecture said.
"Therefore, Lina's work and the exhibition, together, become a stage where the audience get a glimpse of the everyday reality of Brazil in Lina's time."
Other recent exhibitions include a contemporary design show in a neo-gothic house in Belgium and an exhibition about Brasília set within Oscar Niemeyer's Bienal Pavilion in São Paulo .
The photography is by Chen Hao, courtesy of Open Architecture.

The Poetics of Survival is on show at The Power Station of Art, 678 Miaojiang Road, Huangpu District, Shanghai, China 200011 from July 25 to October 25 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

articles.titleOriginal: Reviewing the Aging of the Gut Microbiome and Interventions Known to Improve Its Composition

bodyOriginal.text: The composition of the gut microbiome is influential on long term health and the progression of aging. Unfortunately, this composition changes with age for a range of reasons yet to be fully explored, but which include the decline of the immune system and growing leakage of the intestinal barrier . With age, populations of inflammatory microbial species grow at the expense of microbial species that produce metabolites necessary for tissue function . Studies in short-lived animals suggest that the composition of the gut microbiome is at least as important as lifestyle choices such as level of physical activity when it comes to pace of aging and level of dysfunction in later life.

The means available to manipulate the composition of the gut microbiome are largely not that effective in the grand scheme of things. We know the scope of benefits that arise from a better diet and otherwise better lifestyle choices. Like probiotics , dietary choice can only produce lasting changes in the gut microbiome to some degree, and only if kept up over time. There are one-time treatments that can produce a lasting change in the gut microbiome, however. Flagellin immunization has been explored in animal studies, and provokes the immune system into a lasting campaign to eliminate exactly the sort of undesirable microbial species that increase in number with age. Fecal microbiota transplantation from a young donor into an old recipient resets the composition of the gut microbiome, and in animal studies this improves health and extends life .

In both of these one-time treatments, it is hard to predict exact outcomes. This hinders the development of these therapies for a more widespread use as treatments to reduce the impact of aging by resetting the gut microbiome. More attention is given to fecal microbiota transplantation, with clinical trials accumulating and planned . Nonetheless, the challenges in terms of controlling the inputs and the outcomes of this therapy make it likely that the path ahead will involved the development of artificial gut microbiomes that can be completely controlled and specified. These will form the basis for the next generation of probiotic therapy, capable of replicating some fraction of the effects of fecal microbiota transplantation, and in particular to be capable of producing lasting change in composition.
Gut Microbiota and Ageing: Mechanisms, Age-Related Diseases, and Therapeutic Perspectives

This narrative review synthesised a substantial body of peer-reviewed evidence demonstrating that the gut microbiota undergoes progressive, context-dependent remodelling with advancing age, characterised by reduced taxonomic and functional diversity, depletion of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) -producing taxa , and relative expansion of pathobionts . These changes are increasingly recognised as likely contributors to inflammaging and several hallmarks of ageing , although causal relationships remain incompletely established in humans and likely promote or exacerbate prevalent age-related diseases including neurodegenerative disorders , cardiovascular disease , type 2 diabetes , sarcopenia , osteoporosis , and frailty . Conversely, the distinct microbial configurations observed in centenarians and individuals exhibiting healthy ageing trajectories suggest that maintenance of specific metabolic functionalities (particularly robust SCFA and secondary bile acid pathways) may constitute a feature of successful longevity rather than mere survival bias.

Evidence-based strategies targeting the microbiota, ranging from Mediterranean-style dietary patterns and exercise to precision probiotics, synbiotics , postbiotics , and carefully screened fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), show genuine potential to restore microbial homeostasis , attenuate inflammaging , improve clinical phenotypes , and extend healthspan . Nevertheless, substantial methodological, causal, and translational gaps remain. Overcoming these will require concerted investment in longitudinal multi- omics cohorts, rigorously designed personalised intervention trials, advanced experimental models, and equitable implementation frameworks.

Ultimately, the gut microbiota should be viewed not as a separate entity but as an integral component of the ageing human superorganism. By nurturing microbial ecology throughout life and deploying targeted restoration strategies in later decades, it may become possible to compress morbidity , preserve functional independence, and enable more individuals to reach extreme old age in good health. While the journey from associative observation to causal, personalised, clinically validated interventions remains incomplete, the trajectory is clear: microbiome research represents one of the most promising and rapidly evolving areas within contemporary geroscience . Realising its full potential for human longevity will demand the same rigorous, collaborative, and innovative spirit that has characterised the field's rapid evolution since the advent of high-throughput sequencing.

The next generation of geroscience will increasingly depend on integrating microbial ecology with complementary molecular regulatory systems governing the ageing process, including epigenetic , metabolic , immunological , and post-transcriptional mechanisms. Such multidimensional approaches have the potential to transform microbiome research from a predominantly associative discipline into a mechanistically grounded framework capable of supporting personalised interventions for healthy ageing and longevity.

articles.titleOriginal: AlzeCure’s $12m payday fuels new brain-aging therapy
articles.summaryOriginal: A Danish biotech’s $12 million payment for AlzeCure’s drug platform could reshape the treatment of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. bodyOriginal.text: A Danish biotech’s $12 million payment for AlzeCure’s drug platform could reshape the treatment of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s.

Small biotechs live and die by a brutal math problem: great science, not enough cash to prove it. AlzeCure Pharma , a Stockholm-listed company working on Alzheimer’s and pain, just solved that problem for at least one of its programs, and the way it did so says a lot about how drug development actually gets funded in 2026.

On 12 August, AlzeCure confirmed it had received the full $12 million upfront payment from QuantumCell ApS , a Danish biotech [ 1 ]. The money closes out a licensing deal for AlzeCure’s NeuroRestore platform that the two companies first agreed to back in July. QuantumCell now owns the global rights to NeuroRestore, including its lead candidate, a drug called ACD856. AlzeCure keeps the royalties and a seat on the sidelines.

Here’s what that $12 million actually breaks down to: $7 million in cash for the license itself, plus $5 million that QuantumCell put directly into AlzeCure as an investment. On top of that, the deal includes future milestone payments tied to development and sales, plus royalties that scale up the better the drug performs commercially. Add it all up, excluding royalties, and the agreement could eventually be worth more than $2.2 billion.

That figure will get quoted everywhere, so it’s worth being blunt about what it means. It’s a ceiling, not a check that’s coming in the mail. Biotech licensing deals almost never pay out anywhere close to their headline value, because most of that money is contingent on the drug clearing trials that haven’t happened yet. What actually happened this month is smaller and more concrete: AlzeCure got paid, QuantumCell got the rights and the drug now has a partner with the resources to run the expensive part of drug development that AlzeCure, on its own, likely couldn’t afford.

The reason QuantumCell was willing to pay for this in the first place comes down to how ACD856 actually works. Most Alzheimer’s drugs go after one specific target, usually the amyloid plaques that clump up in the brains of Alzheimer’s patients. ACD856 takes a different route. It boosts two natural signaling pathways that help nerve cells talk to each other, the same pathways involved in forming memories and learning new things. In lab studies, that mechanism improved cognitive function and showed protective effects against inflammation and nerve damage.

What makes it unusual is the range. Because the mechanism isn’t specific to one disease, AlzeCure and now QuantumCell believe it could eventually be tested for Parkinson’s disease and depression as well as Alzheimer’s. That’s a rare position for a single drug candidate to be in, and it’s likely a big part of why the deal came together at all. None of that potential has been proven in a large human trial yet. It’s a reason to watch the drug, not a reason to assume it works.
Martin Jönsson, AlzeCure’s CEO, didn’t undersell the moment.

“The receipt of the upfront payment and completion of the transaction with QuantumCell is a clear testament to the strength of our research and the value represented by NeuroRestore. The platform, including its lead drug candidate ACD856, now has a strong, long-term partner capable of advancing the project for the benefit of multiple patient populations,” he said.

He emphasized the broader significance of the funds, noting that the company anticipates a productive collaboration with QuantumCell for the ongoing development of ACD856 and the NeuroRestore platform. He further explained that the payment received substantially strengthens their financial position while providing greater flexibility to advance their other projects.

AlzeCure has two other research platforms in its pipeline, including a pain program it recently out-licensed to Eli Lilly. This deal isn’t just about NeuroRestore; it’s fuel for everything else the company is trying to keep alive.

Nobody outside biotech circles is going to celebrate a $12 million licensing payment. But this is how the money actually moves in longevity science: small teams do the hard, early work of proving a concept in the lab, then pass the baton and the bill to bigger partners who can afford to run a real clinical trial. Without deals like this, most promising early-stage neuroscience never makes it out of the lab at all.

The target here is a big one. Cognitive decline is arguably the single biggest threat to what people actually want out of a longer life, not just more years, but years spent thinking clearly, recognizing family, and staying independent.

ACD856 hasn’t proven it can deliver that, but a Danish biotech just bet up to $2.2 billion that it might, and that bet is a decent proxy for where serious money in longevity research is currently pointed: at the brain.

articles.titleOriginal: Can AI put the cell back together?
articles.summaryOriginal: GenBio AI’s AIDO Cell links DNA, RNA, protein and cellular behavior – and remembers what’s already happened to the cell. GenBio AI has launched AIDO Cell, a virtual cell system designed to simulate human cellular behavior across multiple biological layers within a single computational environment – allowing researchers to perturb DNA, RNA or proteins and […] The post Can AI put the cell back toget

bodyOriginal.text: GenBio AI’s AIDO Cell links DNA, RNA, protein and cellular behavior – and remembers what’s already happened to the cell.

GenBio AI has launched AIDO Cell, a virtual cell system designed to simulate human cellular behavior across multiple biological layers within a single computational environment – allowing researchers to perturb DNA, RNA or proteins and model how the consequences propagate through to whole-cell behavior.

Built on a world-model architecture, AIDO Cell is also stateful: the simulated cell retains the consequences of previous interventions, allowing sequences of perturbations to accumulate rather than each experiment beginning again from an untouched baseline. Version 1.0 currently supports K562 leukemia and HepG2 liver cancer cell lines, with further cell types in development; the launch follows a Nature Medicine Perspective in which GenBio researchers and collaborators set out a considerably broader vision for connected AI models spanning biological scales.

AIDO Lab is a simulation environment that enables users to explore a coherent, multiomic profile of a virtual cell, generated using AIDO Cell. This example shows virtual staining patterns of proteins in a hepatoblast Hep-G2 model.

Longevity.Technology: Biology has spent several centuries becoming comprehensible by being taken apart. Genes here, proteins there, signaling pathways somewhere in between; reductionism has given us an extraordinary amount of useful science, not because researchers imagined a cell actually operated in neat disciplinary compartments, but because those were the pieces our tools allowed us to hold still long enough to study. The problem is that aging has never been terribly respectful of those boundaries. A perturbation in DNA can alter RNA, protein abundance and cellular behavior; altered cells change their neighbors and tissues, while decades of accumulated insults, adaptations and compensatory responses determine what happens next. Biology has been divided and conquered rather more successfully than it has been reunited – and that is what makes GenBio AI’s AIDO Cell interesting. Its ambition is not simply to build another highly capable biological foundation model, but to connect models across DNA, RNA, protein and whole-cell behavior so that an intervention at one level can propagate through the others, while the system remembers what has already happened.

That last part matters particularly for geroscience. Aging is history-dependent biology; an old cell is not simply a young cell displaying an unfortunate collection of biomarkers, but the present state of a system that has been changing for years. A stateful world model, in which perturbation B acts on the cell left behind by perturbation A rather than repeatedly returning to a pristine computational starting line, is therefore an intriguing proposition. So too is AIDO Cell’s ability to report predicted biological age during a simulation and show that prediction shifting under intervention – although this is precisely where intrigue should acquire a raised eyebrow. A younger predicted age is not necessarily rejuvenation, just as an accurate simulation is not necessarily a causal explanation; what matters is whether those computational changes correspond to reproducible functional changes in wet biology. GenBio’s broader Nature Medicine vision acknowledges many of these hurdles, from causality and uncertainty to benchmarking and experimental validation. The virtual laboratory may eventually let us ask biological questions that reductionism made impractical; the real laboratory, however, still gets to mark the answers.

AIDO Cell sits within GenBio’s broader Artificial Intelligence Digital Organism, or AIDO, program, laid out in a Nature Medicine Perspective co-authored by GenBio’s Le Song, Eran Segal and Eric Xing. In it, the authors argue that biological foundation models have become increasingly capable within individual domains, but remain largely separated by modality and biological scale [ 1 ]. The company’s wider founding team spans computational biology and AI more broadly, including 2024 Chemistry Nobel Laureate David Baker of the University of Washington, Emma Lundberg of Stanford University, Ziv Bar-Joseph of Carnegie Mellon University and Xing himself as GenBio’s president and chief scientist.

AIDO Cell predicts cell-specific molecular signatures. This example shows the epigenetic profile of the albumin gene, which encodes a key protein produced by hepatocytes, in a hepatoblast Hep-G2 model.

Their proposed route toward a digital organism begins pragmatically: build specialist foundation models, connect them across scales and eventually create systems capable of simulating dynamic biological processes from molecules upward. The authors argue that such a framework could offer what they call an “actionable empirical understanding” of biological systems – an ambition that stretches well beyond the present AIDO Cell implementation [ 1 ].

“What’s exciting here isn’t that we’ve solved cellular biology – we haven’t, at least not yet. It’s that, for the first time, we have a system capable of simulating a cell across the full hierarchy of biological scales, from DNA to whole-cell behavior, in one place, which lets you interrogate it computationally,” said Baker. “AIDO Cell is a meaningful foundation to build on, even at this early stage, and could have major implications for fields like drug discovery, toxicology, and disease research broadly.”

The stateful element distinguishes AIDO Cell from simulations in which perturbations are effectively isolated events. A researcher could, for example, alter one component of cellular biology, allow the resulting changes to propagate and then introduce another intervention into that altered state.

“What world model architecture enables, and what makes our system genuinely new, is that it’s both multi-scale and stateful. The simulation remembers what you’ve done to the cell,” said Xing. “You can run entire sequences of perturbations, where each one builds on the last, and see the evolving, cumulative effect in the cell, just as you would in a real (wet lab) workflow.”

AIDO Cell predicts cell-specific molecular signatures. This example shows mRNA isoforms and transcript expression levels of the albumin gene, which encodes a key protein produced by hepatocytes, in a hepatoblast Hep-G2 model.

For aging research, cumulative perturbation is an attractive capability. Cellular aging emerges through interacting changes rather than a single switch; the possibility of interrogating predicted biological age at different points during a sequence could offer a way to explore combinations and ordering of interventions computationally before moving selected hypotheses into experimental systems.

Precisely what those age shifts signify, however, will require careful validation. A model-derived biological age is a prediction generated within a computational representation; demonstrating that its movement corresponds to durable changes in cellular function is a separate task.

GenBio reports an early case study involving imatinib in leukemia cells, in which AIDO Cell recapitulated the drug’s known mechanism and traced the predicted treatment response across the cellular environment. The result provides an initial demonstration of cross-scale simulation, although reproducing a known mechanism is a different challenge from prospectively predicting an unknown one.

AIDO Cell predicts the cell-specific effects of perturbations, including genetic alterations and chemical exposures, which can be chained together within simulations. This example shows differentially expressed genes in a hepatoblast Hep-G2 model following exposure to a novel small molecule generated by AIDO Cell.

That distinction is reflected in the broader AIDO roadmap. In the Nature Medicine Perspective , the authors identify causality, interpretability, uncertainty, bias and generalizability among the unresolved challenges for biological foundation models. Their own benchmark is demanding: predictive accuracy should ultimately approach the intrinsic uncertainty of experimental measurements themselves, with progress expected to arrive incrementally, molecule by molecule before it ever reaches the level of a whole organism [ 1 ].

GenBio itself describes the current release as an early functional preview. “We plan on releasing more advanced versions of the system with enhanced capabilities and accuracy later this year and over the next year,” Xing said.
An early-access collaborator program is also being prepared for researchers in academia, biotechnology and pharma.
The more consequential test will come when AIDO Cell begins making predictions that are not already known – and experimental biology decides whether they survive contact with a real cell.

If connected models can eventually anticipate how sequential interventions reshape cellular state, the virtual cell becomes more than a convenient place to run experiments cheaply; it becomes a machine for deciding which experiments are worth running at all.

Photographs/graphics courtesy of GenBio AI. Main image shows an AIDO Cell-generated novel small-molecule designed to bind protein targets in the context of a cell’s state. This example shows the co-folding of a small molecule designed to bind the HMG co-reductase protein, a key enzyme involved in cholesterol synthesis.
[1] https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04595-0

articles.titleOriginal: Longeveron advances in $101m longevity prize
articles.summaryOriginal: Stem cell data showing durable frailty gains earn Longeveron a $1 million XPRIZE Healthspan milestone award. Part of a ten-part series profiling each of the $101 million XPRIZE Healthspan competition’s Milestone 2 Awardees. Across the series, Longevity.Technology examines the science behind each team’s approach, the trial data supporting it and what stands between them and […] The post Longeveron

bodyOriginal.text: Stem cell data showing durable frailty gains earn Longeveron a $1 million XPRIZE Healthspan milestone award.

Part of a ten-part series profiling each of the $101 million XPRIZE Healthspan competition’s Milestone 2 Awardees . Across the series, Longevity.Technology examines the science behind each team’s approach, the trial data supporting it and what stands between them and the competition’s final phase.

Out of more than 600 teams from 58 countries that entered the XPRIZE Healthspan competition, only ten made it through to Milestone 2. Longeveron , a Miami-based regenerative medicine company, is one of them, and the reason lies in a walking test that most people would barely think twice about.

The XPRIZE Healthspan competition is a seven-year, $101 million global challenge built around a simple premise: develop and test a therapy that can restore muscle, cognition and immune function lost to ageing by at least ten years, ideally twenty, and do it within a year or less of treatment. It is one of the most ambitious prizes in the longevity field, and Longeveron’s path to the finals began with a modest but telling clinical measure, the six-minute walk distance.
A cell therapy built from young donor tissue

Longeveron’s lead candidate, laromestrocel, is an allogeneic mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) therapy derived from the bone marrow of young, healthy adult donors. Unlike therapies that rely on a patient’s own cells, an allogeneic approach uses donor-derived cells manufactured at scale, which is part of what makes it a plausible candidate for the kind of broad, one-time intervention XPRIZE is looking for. The cells are believed to work through several overlapping mechanisms, including anti-inflammatory, pro-vascular and pro-regenerative effects, rather than a single, narrow pathway.

It was published clinical trial data demonstrating that laromestrocel increased six-minute walk distance in patients with aging-related frailty that secured Longeveron’s place among the Milestone 2 Awardees. The six-minute walk test is a standard measure of functional capacity and endurance, and meaningful improvement on it in an older, frail population is a reasonably direct proxy for the kind of functional restoration XPRIZE is designed to reward.
From bone marrow to boardroom: a pipeline built on one platform

What distinguishes Longeveron’s broader story is the breadth of what a single cell platform is being asked to do. The company describes its approach as a “pipeline-in-a-product” strategy, testing laromestrocel across four distinct indications: hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a rare pediatric heart condition, Alzheimer’s disease, pediatric dilated cardiomyopathy and aging-related frailty. That range has already attracted five separate FDA designations, including Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy and Fast Track status for the Alzheimer’s programme as well as Orphan Drug, Fast Track, and Rare Pediatric Disease designations for the heart syndrome programme.

Dr Joshua Hare, Longeveron’s co-founder and chief science officer, pointed to a portfolio of 52 issued patents worldwide that support the platform, alongside positive initial results from five clinical trials across the three indications. For a clinical-stage biotech, that combination of regulatory momentum and intellectual property depth is what makes a multi-indication strategy credible rather than diffuse [ 1 ].

The $1 million award is not the finish line . It funds Longeveron’s participation in the competition’s final phase, where the top-performing teams will run coordinated clinical trials through 2029, competing for a grand prize of up to $81 million. XPRIZE’s evaluators assessed applicants on scientific merit and clinical readiness, screening for the therapies best positioned to demonstrate real restoration of function in adults aged 50 to 90 who are free of major disease, not merely a slowing of decline.

CEO Stephen Willard described the milestone as the start of the competition’s next chapter, one in which Longeveron will continue advancing a therapy the company believes can meaningfully extend healthy life for patients and their families [ 1 ].

Frailty is one of the clearest and most measurable markers of biological aging, and it is also one of the most consequential: loss of muscle function and mobility drives falls, hospitalizations and loss of independence in older adults far more than any single disease diagnosis.

A therapy that can durably restore walking capacity in frail, older patients is a direct assault on one of aging’s most disabling downstream effects. Longeveron’s advancement in a competition explicitly built around restoring lost function, rather than simply extending years lived, reflects where a meaningful share of longevity science is heading: toward interventions judged not by lifespan alone, but by how much of that life remains genuinely functional.

bodyOriginal.alt: Barbican homeware collection by Made.com and Barbican

bodyOriginal.text: Barbican and Made.com have launched a homeware collection According to the Barbican, the collection was developed following research into the original Barbican Estate apartment layouts, including the work of designer Miriam Howitt, who created five show homes for the estate in the 1960s.
The pieces are designed to be used together or independently and prices start from £32.

The collection celebrates architectural details of the iconic London estate "The ambition was to create a complete product range that works both in isolation and together in an open living space," said the Made.com team.
"The final designs reimagine products, graphics and architectural details through a new lens, and into a cohesive product range that captures Barbican living: bold, considered and inherently social."

bodyOriginal.alt: Barbican homeware collection by Made.com and Barbican

bodyOriginal.text: There are chairs with statement wooden side panels The Barbican Estate was designed by Chamberlin, Powell and Bon in the 1950s and opened in 1982. It is one of the largest examples of post-war brutalist architecture in the UK.
Within it is the Barbican Centre – an arts and culture venue with theatres, galleries, cinemas, as well as a conservatory, a library and eateries.

Sofas and textiles feature in the collection A pair of stand-out pieces in the collection is the Curve Table Lamp and Curve Floor Lamp, which have adjustable, tubular shades that draw on the acoustic panels in the Barbican's concert hall.
The lights have chrome bases, with shades available in burgundy, green and blue, contrasted by their fabric cables.
Other lighting pieces include the Coffer ceiling lights and wall lights, which mimic the estate's iconic waffle ceilings, seen throughout its indoor and outdoor spaces.

bodyOriginal.alt: Barbican homeware collection by Made.com and Barbican

bodyOriginal.text: There is a dining set and wall sconces Furniture pieces in the range include the Dual chairs, with statement side panels made of wood and modelled on the estate's concrete pillars, and the modular Plinth coffee table that echoes the sunken seating next to the Barbican lake.
Other furniture pieces include a dining table and chairs, two sofas, and shelving and storage.

Read: Takero Shimazaki Architects infuses Barbican flat with Japanese details Among the accessories is the Brute Rug, which takes visual cues from an original show flat designed by Howitt in 1967, in which she paired plain off-white flats with bold patterned carpets.
It is made from hand-tufted wool with a long shag pile, which the team said was intended "to deliver a retro feel".
A modular coffee table takes cues from the Barbican lake The final pieces in the collection are a series of cushions and textile wall art, each depicting the facades and elevations from the estate.
Warm, neutral tones including mossy greens and rusty oranges are used throughout the collection for a mid-century look, contrasted with stained ash and chrome accents.

bodyOriginal.alt: Barbican homeware collection by Made.com and Barbican

bodyOriginal.text: Storage units also feature in the collection To celebrate the launch, Made.com will be curating an installation at the Barbican Centre from 12 September that both showcases the collection and interiors of homes at the Barbican.

Other Barbican news recently featured on Dezeen includes the upcoming revamp of the complex by British architecture studios Allies and Morrison and Asif Khan Studio , and a 30-tonne earthen installation at the estate by Delcy Morelos, which was informed by a mother's womb .

bodyOriginal.text: Game developer Blue Hood Games has released a survival game named Europe Heatwave Simulator, where players need to outlast a 14-day heatwave without air conditioning in an apartment in Paris .
Playable on the Steam platform, which is downloadable for Windows desktops, Europe Heatwave Simulator challenges players to survive a fortnight in a Parisian apartment in 42-degree Celsius heat.

bodyOriginal.alt: Europe Heatwave Simulator game by Blue Hood Games

bodyOriginal.text: The Europe Heatwave Simulator game takes place in a Parisian apartment In the game, players navigate life without air conditioning, tending to the needs of their overheating body by keeping cool, hydrated and fed, while also working a remote job from a laptop on the dining table.
Blue Hood Games described Europe Heatwave Simulator as a "dark humour" game centred on "the crushing reality of modern European summers without air conditioning".

bodyOriginal.alt: Europe Heatwave Simulator game by Blue Hood Games

bodyOriginal.text: Players can order supplies from a company called Greedco Featuring a low-polygon graphic style modelled on early PlayStation games, key decisions in the gameplay include whether to open windows and let mosquitoes in or keep them shut and sacrifice natural airflow.
Players can also order overpriced fans, ice packs and gadgets from a company named Greedco, which bears a swooshing arrow logo similar to that of online retailer Amazon .

Read: "Human refrigerator" provides escape from deadly heatwaves In a trailer for Europe Heatwave Simulator, Blue Hood Games described the game as "based on real events" while showing a portion where players race and battle against shoppers to get their hands on air conditioning units, which takes place in a supermarket with branding akin to Lidl.

Severe heatwaves have continued to affect countries across Europe this summer. France experienced record-breaking temperatures in May and June, which contributed to the subsequent spread of wildfires in the country.

articles.titleOriginal: Eight pavilion highlights from Jia Curated 2026
articles.summaryOriginal: The fifth edition of Bali's Jia Curated design festival features pavilions that aim to put nature at the centre, including structures built from rice husks and salt bricks. Here are eight of the most interesting. Taking place from 13 to 17 August, this year's Jia Curated showcased craft and design works from Indonesia across Asia The post Eight pavilion highlights from Jia Curated 2026 appeared fi

bodyOriginal.text: The fifth edition of Bali 's Jia Curated design festival features pavilions that aim to put nature at the centre, including structures built from rice husks and salt bricks. Here are eight of the most interesting.
Taking place from 13 to 17 August, this year's Jia Curated showcased craft and design works from Indonesia across Asia including participants from Philippine, Japan and Taiwan.
The festival's new venue at Pengembak Beach in Sanur on Bali's eastern shoreline informed this year's theme – Nature Weave.
The pavilions were each designed to respond to the landscape, creating experiences that allowed materials, objects and structures to actively engage with the surrounding environment.

Each pavilion also combined pieces and input from multiple brands. According to Jia Curated co-founder Budiman Ong, the spirit of mutual co-operation followed the Indonesian principle of Gotong Royong – collective effort.

"We are interested in creating the conditions for spontaneous encounters, encouraging conversation and allowing different disciplines, materials, practices and perspectives to exist alongside one another," said Ong.

"Ultimately, Jia Curated is not simply about showcasing individual works," he continued. |It is about building connection, between designers, craftspeople, brands, institutions and communities across Indonesia and beyond."
Read on for more about the top eight pavilions:
The Intelligence of Surfaces, by DDAP Architect for Lamitak
Local architecture studio DDAP Architect designed the pavilion for decorative high-pressure laminates manufacturer Lamitak to evoke unfolding origami.
The front of the pavilion folded inward, naturally marking the entrance as well as forming a public gathering area.
Perorated timber facade allowed free flow of air within the space, while also doubled as displays for product samples.
The Internal layout followed the journey of how natural paper engineered and crafted into decorative surface, with exisiting landscape integrated into the spacial experience.
Trees punctured the roof, and natural rocks became seatings, creating a conversation between nature, material, and architecture.

"More than an exhibition, the pavilion is an invitation to navigate a new perspective, to questions assumptions, uncover hidden value, and discover that the most meaningful stories often lie beneath the surface," said DDAP Architect.
Photo by Indra Wiras Sraya, by ATMA for Suaru
Named after the Sanskrit word for shelter, local architecture studio ATMA designed the pavilion for independent furniture brand Suaru to foster a sense of comfort, order and belonging.

The pavilion was arranged into a series of zones that was informed by Asta Kosala Kosali – a spacial philosophy used in a typical Balinese home. It categorises spaces from most to least sacred, combined with the directional axes of north to south and east to west, positioned around a central courtyard.
Objects were placed throughout the pavilion according to the roles traditionally assigned to each space, creating a subtle dialogue between the objects and their architectural setting.
Main Main, by Blanco Studio and Bali Landscape Company
Balinese architecture practice Blanco Studio 's pavilion aimed to awaken the nostalgic memories of childhood playtime.
Four raw teak slabs by custom woodworking atelier Kalpa Taru formed a series of communal tables at the centre, on which game boards were free to play.
The studio designed a structure from timber offcuts that rose above the tables to form a tree-like canopy that sheltered the visitors.

"Like the trees we once gathered beneath, it provides shade, shelter and a sense of wonder," said Blanco Studio. "It evokes the simple joy of outdoor play and the quiet nostalgia of childhood afternoon spent together —moments of connection, imagination, and discovery held beneath a protected canopy of nature."
Photo by Indra Wiras Suar, by Studio Aliri

Indonesia design practice Studio Aliri designed Suar to reference the limited land available in densely populated Indonesian cities and show how spatial richness can be achieved with a limited footprint.

The structure was built on a plot of 2.4 metres long and 4.8 metres wide, with four viewing platforms stacked above one another, all pointing towards the ocean. The first level platform was extended further to connect to the Penjor – a tall, curved bamboo pole used in Balinese Hindu ceremony.
The pavilion was constructed from rubberwood glulam, with safety railings made from woven rattan.
After the festival, the pavilion will be relocated to Medewi Beach in Bali to be permanently used as a public lookout.
Photo by Christina Yao Bhumi Lingsir, by Nawangseta, in collaboration with Living Designs Bali
Bali-based architecture studio Nawangseta designed a sequence of spaces informed by traditional Balinese architecture.
The journey began in a space symbolising purity before gradually leading towards areas that represented complexity, duality and the many choices encountered throughout life.

A hundred traditional Balinese Topeng Buduh masks were added to signify the many faces of human nature; sand on the ground embodied both strength and fragility; and water falling from the rain chains symbolised the element that connects all life forms.
"Architectural elements do more than define physical boundaries they communicate philosophical ideas about the relationship between humanity, nature, and spirituality," said Nawangseta.
Constructed from Himalayan salt bricks from Tuscany Stone Boutique , the Oaken Tiltroom pavilion was partially embedded into the ground.
Designed by Jakarta-based design practice Spatial Sonata , the pavilion aimed to create a contemplative environment shaped by landscape and sensory design.
Inside, the pavilion featured Oaken 's fragrances as well as Stillroom 's botanical drinks, with the aim of engaging all senses.
Alunan Pesisir, by Vivere Group and Eugenio Hendro
Indonesian interiors brand Vivere Group and furniture designer Eugenio Hendro presented a pavilion that aimed to explore the living rhythm of Bali's ever-changing coastline.

Made from glulam, the structure was topped with a curved roof. The ceiling was covered in a blue carpet, while a combination of natural rattan and acoustic panels made by recycled materials formed the side barriers.
The interplay of light and shadow completed the experience where material, form, atmosphere and movement flow as one.
Created by Indonesian furniture designer Eugenio Hendro , the Tapak Tumbuh pavilion was organised into three chapters: earth, harvest and vegetation.

Ceramic surfaces by Singres tiles, informed by soil formation and agricultural terrain, captured the natural colour and texture of the earth. Decking, facade and walls were made primarily from rice husks and recycled plastic supplied by Plana .
Moire Rugs transformed vegetation by translating the growth of roots, leaves, and organic forms into experimental textile patterns. Large scale rugs spread across the space like living organism.

"From soil with natural hues, sediments and textures. From rices as it grows, harvested, and returns to the land. From roots, leaves, and vegetation that continue to spread and evolve," said Hendro. "These cycles are reinterpreted into surfaces, structures, textiles and spacial experience, each shaped through human hands as an essential catalyst."
The photography is by David Wilson unless otherwise stated.
Jia Curated 2026 took place from 13 to 17 August 2026 at Pengembak Beach in Bali. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

"The concept behind the Devil's Milk project was to investigate The post Shahar Livne's The Devil's Milk furniture explores

bodyOriginal.text: Designer Shahar Livne has created The Devil's Milk, a collection of designs that investigate rubber production and its history of violence and abuse.
The designs, which Livne created over two years, include a scale, a cabinet and a bench, made from different types of rubber.

A scale is among the designs by Shahar Livne "The concept behind the Devil's Milk project was to investigate the history of rubber production and its material, political, and social cultures," Livne told Dezeen.

"Rubber production and extraction have a long history of abuse and violence, and that is almost forgotten when we see rubber in everyday context," she continued. "Rubber is an essential part of many products and technologies; it has shaped human culture far more than it gets credit for."

A cabinet features bark from a rubber tree Livme sourced the natural latex for the scales and the rubber used for the cabinet from Indonesia, while the bench was made from synthetic rubber used in the film industry.
"During the two years of working on the project, I found many parallels between the human body and the botanical body of the rubber tree," she explained.

"I focused on the idea of botanical kinship – the relationship, indigenous knowledge and spiritual connections humans have with rubber, in this case natural rubber from rubber plants, but also the place of synthetic rubbers in pop culture and fetish, such as in the movie industry."

It also has rubber from Indonesia and explores the material's colonial roots All of the pieces were designed to involve rubber in different ways. For the cabinet, Livne used wood from the bark of the rubber tree Heave Brislius, which is considered cheap wood and has many imperfections.
"I wanted not only to highlight and elevate the expressiveness of the scars and character of the wood in the furniture piece; it is also symbolic," Livne said.

"The wood inlays decorating the cabinet are made of European, African, Indonesian and South American wood species – all places where rubber wood was extracted from or exported to, and by embedding them in the rubber wood, they 'colonise' it."

Read: Shahar Livne designs fossil-like jewellery for Balenciaga from ocean plastic For the bench, which was designed to resemble a log, Livne chose a synthetic engineered rubber material. This was designed to mimic human skin and is used in special effects for props and costumes.
"I used the technique of painting and creating textures in the rubber to create a transition between a human and a tree," Livne said.
"It is inspired by the idea of botanical kinship, the philosophical and ecological world-view that recognises plants as our biological and spiritual relatives rather than mere resources."

The Devil's Milk also includes a bench resembling a log She aimed for the piece to challenge "the colonial 'plant blindness' of Western-centric hierarchies that view nature as passive or inferior," Livne said.
"In the many places where the rubber tree grows naturally, such as in the Congo, Borneo and the Amazon, the relationship with the forest is historically spiritual," she continued.
"It is a living space where trees hold divine forces. Here, collecting from the forest is not an 'economic activity'; it is a social interaction with a conscious, sacred environment."
The bench is covered in skin-like synthetic rubber With the scales, Livne wanted to symbolise the economic force of rubber, which she says at one point was compared in its value to precious metals.
"It was aggressively extracted to fuel global industrialisation during the rubber boom in the 19th and 20th centuries," Livne said.

"However, this immense wealth relied entirely on brutal exploitation; raw yields were strictly weighed on scales to enforce strict labour quotas and control Indigenous populations, deforming their bodies."
The scale symbolises the economic force of rubber The title of her project comes from author John Tully's book The Devil's Milk: A social history of rubber, which Livne used as part of her research.
She is currently working on a publication based on her research together with curator Yev Kravt and design studio Droog , who hosted a symposium on rubber with Livne last year.
Livne was named emerging designer of the year at Dezeen Awards 2020 and has previously designed fossil-like jewellery from ocean plastic and trainers from slaughterhouse waste .

articles.summaryOriginal: Designerly’s Cooper Adwin explains why the ‘Biological Age’ metric Is threatening to derail longevity venture capital. bodyOriginal.text: Designerly’s Cooper Adwin explains why the ‘Biological Age’ metric Is threatening to derail longevity venture capital.

Longevity venture capital is experiencing a breakout moment, with billions flowing into companies developing proprietary biological age clocks. Companies position epigenetic, proteomic and transcriptomic dashboards as the gold standard for measuring intervention efficacy. Yet beneath the hype lies a regulatory cliff. Without clinically validated endpoints, the sector risks a credibility collapse and widespread investor exodus.
The valuation disconnect in modern geroscience

The longevity sector is absorbing unprecedented levels of investment. Q1 2026 alone brought in approximately $3.74 billion , a 56% surge year-over-year. Venture capitalists (VCs) are backing proprietary biological age diagnostics [ 1 ]. Many startups claim, even without clinical validation, that their algorithm outperforms the competition.

The enthusiasm makes sense. Quantifying aging at the molecular level represents genuine scientific progress. However, the valuations rest on assumptions about therapeutic applications that remain unproven. As investor expectations collide with the realities of drug development, this disconnect will reshape capital allocation across the geroscience sector.
Why proprietary biomarker dashboards fail clinical scrutiny

Competing companies have flooded the market with siloed paradigms that do not align. Epigenetic, proteomic and transcriptomic approaches measure DNA methylation [ 2 ], protein levels and gene expression. None shares a common measurement framework, preventing meaningful cross-trial comparisons or reliable outcome predictions.

Epigenetic markers and disease require rigorous scrutiny to demonstrate that they reflect genuine biological decline [ 3 ]. Without that proof, these tools lack the causal relationships regulators demand for therapeutic approval.

Consumer-facing dashboards excel at improving data literacy , which can help patients as they try to understand their health metrics. A sleek interface and personalized recommendations can engage users and drive behavior change, but design polish cannot substitute for rigorous science. Investors counting on direct-to-consumer revenue without Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval strategies face a reckoning.
The FDA roadblock threatening capital allocation
Once Series A backers recognize that portfolio companies cannot advance therapeutics through Phase III trials, expect rapid capital flight. The longevity space already lived through this in 2020.

The senolytics hype cycle collapsed following UNITY Biotechnology’s high-profile Phase II trial failure . UNITY’s market value fell sharply after UBX0101 failed to separate from placebo in a Phase II osteoarthritis trial, prompting the company to cut its lead program. Without regulatory wins, expect the same correction for biological age metrics.

Regulators use strict criteria to evaluate medical interventions, but longevity biomarkers currently fail to meet them. Under FDA-aligned surrogate-endpoint frameworks, a validated surrogate must be supported by a mechanistic rationale and clinical evidence showing that movement in the surrogate predicts clinical benefit [ 4 ]. Think of hemoglobin A1c for diabetes and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol for cardiovascular events.

Most biological-aging assays have not yet reached that bar – recent reviews note that the field still lacks consensus validation standards [ 5 ], cross-population generalizability and sufficient evidence for clinical translation as surrogate endpoints.

The FDA does not recognize aging as a disease. Without disease classification, companies cannot leverage surrogate markers to accelerate therapeutic development. This creates a fundamental bottleneck. Billions in VC funding remain trapped in ventures that cannot satisfy approval requirements.
Transitioning from consumer apps to clinical disease models

The strategic pivot demands disease-first development. Sustainable business models must first develop medicines and diagnostics for established, FDA-recognized indications before expanding into broader preventive uses. Cardiovascular outcomes, metabolic dysfunction and neurodegenerative decline all offer established approval frameworks where biomarker development can proceed under current regulations.

Building clinical evidence for a specific condition opens access to broader applications. Once an assay demonstrates predictive value for cardiovascular outcomes or cognitive decline, the route to general healthspan claims becomes viable. Founders prioritizing direct-to-consumer revenue sacrifice long-term viability for short-term cash flow. Some may not make the pivot until forced.
Establishing consensus metrics to protect industry valuations

Averting a sector-wide market correction requires a shift from proprietary black-box algorithms to standardized, collaborative biomarker frameworks. Current fragmentation sacrifices industry wide credibility for the advantage of individual vendors, eroding trust among regulators and institutional allocators alike.

Consensus frameworks preserve competition while establishing shared standards for trial comparisons, faster regulatory reviews and sectoral legitimacy. The alternative means each company independently burns capital to establish what should be common knowledge. The industry cannot afford this unsustainable approach.
Securing the future of biotech investments

The winners will be those who recognize where true leverage exists. Firms must align development programs with approval frameworks. Investors must evaluate clinical substance over marketing narratives. Founders must be willing to invest five years building disease-specific evidence before claiming broader applications.

Biological age assays hold genuine promise, but only if the industry confronts its clinical evidence gap before investor patience runs out. Smart capital recognizes that the route forward requires disease-specific applications, transparent methodologies and a willingness to prioritize scientific rigor over proprietary positioning. The sector’s maturation depends on it.

Cooper Adwin is an Assistant Editor at Designerly Magazine with 5+ years of experience writing on B2B technology, data analytics, and AI applications. He focuses on breaking down complex technological developments, compliance, and data-driven trends for B2B audiences.

articles.titleOriginal: What the body’s early warning system is really telling us
articles.summaryOriginal: New biomarkers promise early disease detection, but doctors using them daily struggle to weigh the value of these warnings. For Dr Alexandru Ardelean, a specialist in internal medicine at Years, it was a pattern, rather than a single moment. Working […] The post What the body’s early warning system i

bodyOriginal.text: New biomarkers promise early disease detection, but doctors using them daily struggle to weigh the value of these warnings.

There’s a kind of frustration that drives people out of conventional medicine and into prevention. For Dr Alexandru Ardelean, a specialist in internal medicine at Years , it was a pattern, rather than a single moment. Working in the ER, he kept seeing the same cardiology patients cycle back through, and he started asking a question that traditional medicine isn’t built to answer: when did this actually start?

That question is the thread running through this week’s episode of Longevity Technology UNLOCKED , where hosts Dr Nina Patrick and Longevity.Technology CEO Phil Newman sit down with Ardelean and Jürgen Mehrtens, the clinician and CEO, respectively, behind Years, a Berlin-based longevity clinic betting its entire model on one idea: that the body sends out distress signals long before disease shows up on a chart.
Two signals, in particular, are getting a lot of attention right now: GDF-15 and P-tau217. Neither is a household name yet. Both might be soon.

Think of GDF-15 less as a diagnosis and more as your body’s smoke detector; it doesn’t tell you what’s burning, only that something is. Ardelean describes it as a marker of generalized cellular stress, produced across a huge range of tissues in response to everything from mitochondrial dysfunction to chronic inflammation. It’s already used clinically to help predict heart failure outcomes and, notably, in oncology, where it’s linked to the appetite loss seen in cancer cachexia – one reason a pharmaceutical company has developed an antibody specifically targeting it.

But its pull into longevity medicine came from a different body of research: studies showing GDF-15 tracks closely with chronological age, and that its trend over time, not a single snapshot, predicts mortality and illness down the line.

As Ardelean put it: “we do not use these biomarkers as of yet in preventative medicine to build the therapeutic strategy. We use them in order to measure the therapeutic success,” meaning a high reading doesn’t hand you a treatment plan. It tells you whether the plan you’re already on is working.

What made this conversation refreshing is that it didn’t oversell the science. Pressed on whether these markers throw off false positives, Ardelean’s answer wasn’t reassuring in the way marketing usually is; it was more useful than that.

“My concern is not necessarily about false positives, it’s about false negatives,” he said, describing patients whose P-tau217, a marker tied to early Alzheimer’s risk, came back elevated but who showed no cognitive symptoms, no genetic risk and scored well on testing. In those cases, the clinic leans on repeated measurement over time rather than reacting to one number.

There’s no settled reference range for GDF-15 in preventive use either; it can swing from 300 to 600 in a perfectly healthy 40-year-old. Ardelean even floated a working theory mid-interview, coining the idea of a “cellular stress reserve,” the notion that some people’s healthy habits may be buying them a buffer that keeps the number looking normal even as underlying strain builds. It’s a hypothesis, not a finding, and he said as much. That kind of transparency is rare, and it’s worth more to patients than false certainty.

The business model behind Years is arguably the more provocative part of this story. Mehrtens set out to build a longitudinal dataset, and realized the only way to guarantee data quality was to own the clinics generating it. Every client runs through an identical diagnostic protocol, repeated annually, no menu nor shortcuts. The pitch to future partners, including pharmaceutical companies, is a dataset clean enough to accelerate drug development.
It’s a bet that consistency beats convenience and a quiet rebuke of a healthcare system Mehrtens doesn’t hesitate to criticize.
“Our healthcare system is broken,” he said flatly, adding that it’s likely true across most Western countries, Germany and the UK included.

What stood out beyond the biomarkers was how much of Years’ actual retention strategy is built on community – running clubs, book readings, patients sharing their own turnaround stories with each other. It’s an implicit acknowledgment that data alone doesn’t change behavior; belonging might. As competitors in the functional medicine space struggle with client retention because, in Mehrtens’ words, patients often “don’t see or feel a difference,” Years is betting that visible, trackable progress – paired with people cheering each other on – is what keeps someone coming back for their next blood draw.

Predictive biomarkers won’t replace the boring fundamentals – sleep, movement, nutrition – anytime soon. But they might finally give people a reason to take them seriously before the ER visit, not after.

bodyOriginal.text: Seven existing colourways have been rethought, while nine new shades have been released Existing colours Bianco, Tortora, Mattone, Celeste, Pistacchio, Perla and Nero are joined by nine new shades: Sabbia, Limone, Corallo, Borgogna, Cannella, Oltremare, Alloro, Calce and Gru.

Looking to protect the natural landscape as much as possible, Woźniczka – a co-founder of studio KameleonLab – chose to "deliberately limit" the scheme's footprint.
The design left 85 per cent of the site untouched and restricted construction to existing clearings and meadows.

Kuba Woźniczka has completed a series of holiday cabins in Poland "From the outset, the ambition was not to maximise the site's development potential, but to create a place that would coexist with the surrounding landscape instead of dominating it," the architect told Dezeen.
"The brief focused less on a specific architectural language and more on the values the project should represent: restraint, longevity and respect for the site's existing natural character," he said.
"Although planning regulations would have permitted much denser development, a significant portion of the site was deliberately left untouched, with not a single tree being cut down."

bodyOriginal.alt: Exterior view of timber-clad cabin by Kuba Woźniczka

bodyOriginal.text: Each cabin offers 85-square-metres of living space Each of the mono-pitched cabins offers 85 square metres of living space across two storeys.
A living, dining and kitchen area sits alongside a bedroom and bathroom on the ground floor, with an additional bedroom and bathroom upstairs.

bodyOriginal.alt: Open-plan living area at Studzienno 27 holiday home

bodyOriginal.text: The living, dining and kitchen spaces are held on the ground floor Built from cross-laminated timber (CLT), the cabins were oriented to capture views from a balcony and decked patio, while avoiding disruption to any existing trees or vegetation.
Contrasting their exteriors, which are clad in planks of blackened timber, the pale CLT structure has been left exposed throughout the interiors.
Read: HOLA Design builds gabled lakeside cottage in Poland The interiors were designed by Wrocław-based interior design practice Madde Studio to create a feeling of "calm and immersion".

Exposed timber walls and ceilings are complemented by pale pastel green tones, with darker green metal frames surrounding the large windows, which have discreet bird-safe markings to minimise collisions.
Alongside areas of bespoke timber carpentry, such as in the kitchens and bathrooms, Madde Studio also sourced a series of vintage and second-hand furniture pieces.

bodyOriginal.alt: Bedroom interior at residence by Kuba Woźniczka

bodyOriginal.text: Its exposed structure contrasts with a blackened exterior "Rather than resisting the natural ageing process of timber, the project embraces it, allowing the buildings to evolve alongside the surrounding landscape," said Madde Studio.
"Furnishings follow the same philosophy, combining natural materials with carefully selected second-hand furniture and vintage pieces that bring an existing history into the project," it added.

bodyOriginal.alt: Stairway within the Studzienno 27 cabin by Kuba Woźniczka

bodyOriginal.text: The interiors feature pastel green details Other holiday retreats in Poland include a duo of cottages overlooking the Silesian Beskids mountains by architecture studio Mistovia, and a gabled lakeside cottage by HOLA Design .

bodyOriginal.text: The first production model of the electric Ferrari designed by Jony Ive and Marc Newson has sold for $40 million – a record price for a new vehicle at auction.
The carmaker's polarising first foray into EVs, the Ferrari Luce , went under the hammer as part of a RM Sotheby's charity auction at Monterey Car Week in California.

bodyOriginal.alt: Side view of Ferrari Luce Chassis 0 from RM Sotheby

bodyOriginal.text: The first production model of the Ferrari Luce went under the hammer at RM Sotheby's The design, courtesy of former Apple designers Jony Ive and Marc Newson, proved controversial when it launched in May , with some commenters arguing that the design does not look enough like a Ferrari with its pared-back silhouette, four doors and five seats.

Pre-auction estimates suggested that the special-edition all-white Ferrari Luce would bring in $1.1 million at Sotheby's. But it went on to fetch $40 million (£29.6 million) – more than 60 times its already lofty retail price.
It marks a new record for a new car sold at auction, with all proceeds from the sale going towards educational initiatives through The Ferrari Foundation, Sotheby's said.

bodyOriginal.alt: Interior of special edition all-white Ferrari EV

bodyOriginal.text: The special-edition all-white model sold for $40m After the launch in May, Ferrari's share price initially dropped by eight per cent amid criticism over its design.
Among the critics was Ferrari's former chairman Luca di Montezemolo, who led the carmaker for 23 years until 2014.
"We're risking the destruction of a legend, and I'm truly sorry about that," he told Italian media. "I hope they at least remove the prancing horse."

Read: Why does everyone seem to hate the new electric Ferrari? Nevertheless, Ferrari sold out its entire 2026 target within only two months of launch, the Financial Times reported . The first of these cars will be delivered to customers in October, the company said last ​year.

"There are an enormous number of people who are just predisposed to not want to like this," Newson told Dezeen at the Luce's launch in May . "They haven't even seen the thing, let alone driven the thing."
"But the reality is people need to drive this car to really, really understand it, and I would urge people, before they pass those sorts of judgments, to try it."

bodyOriginal.alt: Rear view of Ferrari Luce Chassis 0 from RM Sotheby

bodyOriginal.text: It marks a record for a new car sold at auction In many ways, the Ferrari Luce is a meeting of giants. Former Apple design boss Jony Ive and his longtime collaborator Marc Newson are, in their own right, two of the most influential industrial designers of our time.
And the car is the first to be designed by the duo as part of their joint studio LoveFrom , which they founded after leaving Apple in 2019 .
Newson is no stranger to setting records at auction. The Australian industrial designer is also responsible for creating the most expensive furniture piece ever sold at auction by a living designer .
